title: From Danville's furnaces to Vancouver Island's coal: Cecilia McGuire Dunn
body:
In 1870 Edward McGuire, an Irish immigrant, was a furnace helper at Danville, Montour County, home of the Montour Iron Works. His children, among them James (Kathryn McGuire's grandfather) and a five-year-old daughter the census-taker spelled "Mesilla", soon followed the work north to the coal towns of Plymouth.

Cecilia ("Scylia" on her licence) married a young Plymouth man, Murdock Dunn, at Plymouth at the end of December 1886/87. Within a few years the couple had joined the stream of Pennsylvania anthracite miners who went to the coal mines of Vancouver Island. By the 1901 Canadian census they were living at South Wellington near Nanaimo, British Columbia. Murdock died that year, leaving Cecilia with young children; she remarried at Ladysmith in 1908 and died there in 1918. Her brother James stayed in Plymouth and Larksville; her sister Mary, widowed at 33, raised six children in Plymouth.

sourceRefs.citation: FamilySearch tree G3FP-1G7
Luzerne Co. Marriage License Docket no. 1790
1870 census Mahoning Twp

title: Searching the border skies: Maj. Leo Heffernan's rescue flights and record dash
body:
Before the speed record that made national headlines, Leo Heffernan's job at Fort Bliss included hunting for lost fliers over some of the emptiest country in North America. In February 1921, as commander of aviation at Fort Bliss, he flew to Sanderson, Texas, to organise flying expeditions over the Big Bend and into Chihuahua for Lt. Alexander Pearson, missing since the previous Thursday. In December 1922 he led five planes of the 12th Observation Squadron west toward Tucson to join the search for Col. Francis Marshall and Lt. Charles Webber.

In March 1923, flying a DH-4B from Nogales back to Fort Bliss, he ran into a sandstorm at Columbus, New Mexico, with the air full of sand up to 6,000 feet and a gale of more than 100 mph behind him. He covered the 75 miles to El Paso in 18 minutes, about 250 mph. The San Antonio Light called it the best speed in the world, but noted that the flight was "not official".

sourceRefs.citation: Evening Public Ledger (Philadelphia), 14 Feb 1921, p.4
Bismarck Tribune, 9 Dec 1922, p.1
San Antonio Light, 24 Mar 1923, p.1

title: Twice-linked families: the Jones-McGuire-McAvoy weddings in Plymouth
body: Kathryn McGuire's parents were joined by three earlier marriages. About 1884 James McGuire married Anna C. Jones, an English-born daughter of the Welsh miner Edward F. Jones. On 29 Dec 1914 Anna's younger brother Joseph S. Jones, a 33-year-old mine headman, married Agnes M. McAvoy at Plymouth before Rev. P. J. Colligan. Their docket records Joseph's mother's maiden name as "Kiver" and Agnes's mother, Catharine Murphy, as born in Schuylkill County. Agnes's widowed mother had meanwhile married another Jones, John H. Nine years later, on 20 Jun 1923, the same priest married Agnes's sister Elizabeth McAvoy to Anna's son Frank J. McGuire. Frank's bride was thus already his uncle's sister-in-law.

sourceRefs.citation: Luzerne Co. Marriage License Docket no. 71238 (1914)
Luzerne Co. marriage licence no. 635 (1923)

title: 1028 Bunker Hill Street: a grocer's house becomes the family compound
body:
John Petriello's grocery stood on Bunker Hill, the slope on the Scranton–Dunmore line where emigrants from Guardia Lombardi settled. In 1910 the family lived at 1030 Ash Street, and by 1920 at 1028 Bunker Hill Street, which John owned free of mortgage, giving his occupation as merchant, grocery store. John died in April 1939, four years after his wife Maria Antonia, and the house stayed in the family. When the census-taker came in April 1940, three of his sons were renting separate units at no. 1028: James with his wife Mollie and children John (Sharon Meier's father, aged 7) and Ann Marie; Nicholas with Genevieve and a baby; and Charles with Elsie.

The rest of the block was family too. At no. 1015 his daughter Grace and her husband Joseph DiBiasi lived above a general grocery that Grace herself ran. At no. 1003 his daughter Josephine Castellano lived with her railroad-car-repairer husband and three children. DiBiasi cousins (the widow of Maria Antonia's brother Domenico Antonio, a widowed Vincenzo DiBiasi, and others) lived at nos. 1009 and 1022. A Genello family lived at no. 1020; Ann Marie later married a Genello. After the war James moved his family a few blocks into Dunmore, to 128 Sand Street, near his wife's widowed mother.

title: Grace Petrillo DiBiasi: an American who had to be 'repatriated'
body:
Grace was born in Pennsylvania in January 1897, but in June 1943 she stood before the federal court in Scranton to regain her American citizenship. Under the Expatriation Act of 1907, an American woman who married a foreign national automatically lost her citizenship. Grace had married Joseph DiBiasi, an Italian-born neighbour from Bunker Hill, at a time when that law still applied (the 1922 Cable Act ended it), so she had become an alien in her own country. Her index card is marked 'Rep.' for repatriation, certificate 250, and gives her birthplace simply as 'U.S.A.'.

In the 1940 census it was Grace, not her husband, who was listed as the merchant running a general grocery store at 1015 Bunker Hill Street, a few doors from where her father John had kept his grocery for decades.

title: Sand Street, Dunmore: the Giannettas from Bisaccia
body:
Frank Giannetta came from the Irpinian shepherd town of Bisaccia to New York on the SS Italia in 1903, and his wife Angelica followed in 1909 with their four children. By April 1910 the family was at 134 Sand Street in Dunmore, where Frank worked as a contractor's laborer. Carmela, who would become 'Mollie' Petriello, was born there in July 1910, three months after that census. By 1920 Frank owned no. 133 and worked in the railroad shops, while his two eldest sons, Sam and Marion, worked at a coal breaker. Sand Street was a close neighbourhood: son Joseph married Vincenza Gillette from next door at no. 135, at St. Rocco's church in 1933.

Frank died in April 1934. Angelica, a foundling from Sant'Angelo dei Lombardi with no known parents, kept the house. She was still there in April 1950, aged 75 and by then a naturalized citizen, living with her son Anthony, a WWII Army veteran. Her daughter Mollie's family lived at no. 128, and her daughter Mary Pichiarello, whose husband ran a grocery, lived next door to them.

title: The burial waves of 1668-69 and 1712 in San Mango
body:
Counting the San Mango d'Aquino parish burial index by year shows two mortality crises. In 1668 and 1669 the priest recorded 49 and 52 burials, several times the usual 10-30. Among them were John's ancestors Gerolimo Cicco, Gio Domenico and Santa Rizzo (all within a fortnight in August-September 1668) and Salvatore Piraijna.

In 1712 the register records 129 burials, 53 of them in December alone. Angila Vaccaro died in January; Vittoria Ragona on 27 November; Fabio Manfrida on 8 December; and Ottavio Putero on 23 December. The cause is not stated in the index; the winter clustering points to an epidemic.

D. Lupia and J. Bifano/Epifano), sheet '1653-1671 and 1687-1713'.

title: Two Ferlaino lines meet: pedigree collapse behind Helen Ferlaino
body:
Helen (Maria Filomena) Ferlaino, born at San Mango on 8 October 1894, had parents who were already related. Her father Leopoldo descended from Nicola Maria Ferlaino (b. 1778); her mother Giuseppina Fiorillo descended, through Giuseppina Ferlaino (b. 1811), from Nicola's younger brother Vincenzo (b. 1781). Both brothers were sons of Bruno Ferlaino and Francesca Moraca, married in 1777.

A second loop runs through the Moracas: Agata Moraca (Leopoldo's grandmother) and her brother Alessio (Giuseppina's great-great-grandfather) were both children of Michele Moraca and Anna Maria Puteri. In a village of a few hundred families this was normal, but it means several San Mango couples appear twice in John's pedigree.

D. Lupia and J. Bifano/Epifano), sheet '1767-1808'.

title: From Cannovali to San Mango: the Fiorillos come down the Savuto
body:
The Fiorillos were not San Mango people. Domenico (Gabriele) Fiorillo was born about 1775 at Cannovali, a hamlet of Aiello Calabro up the Savuto valley; his son Carmine was born at Savuto about 1806, and daughters Cintia and Antonia at Aiello. By 1839 the family was in San Mango, where Carmine married Giuseppina Ferlaino in March 1840.

The 1840 marriage act names Carmine's mother as Maria Marrelli, then living. Twenty years later his death record called her 'Vittoria', the name of his aunt by marriage (wife of Francesco Gabriele Fiorillo). This is how the tree acquired 'Vittoria Marrelli' as a direct ancestor.

title: Two First Ladies of 'Tippecanoe and Tyler Too'
body:
The Whig ticket of 1840 put William Henry Harrison and John Tyler into the White House, and both of their wives turn out to be John's cousins, through different branches of his Long Island ancestry. Anna Symmes Harrison descended from the Southold Tuthills and Wellses: her great-great-grandfather Justice Henry Tuthill was the brother of John's ancestor John Tuthill Jr, and his wife Bethia Horton was a granddaughter of William Wells. Anna never reached Washington; her husband died a month after the inauguration, and their grandson Benjamin Harrison became president in 1889.

Tyler's second wife, Julia Gardiner, descended from Bull Smith of Smithtown through Richard Smith 2d, his son Nathaniel, and Nathaniel's daughter Mary, who married Col. Abraham Gardiner of East Hampton. Julia's father, Senator David Gardiner, was killed on 28 Feb 1844 when the 'Peacemaker' gun exploded aboard USS Princeton while the president was aboard; Tyler and Julia married quietly in New York four months later.

sourceRefs.citation: Lucy D. Akerly, The Tuthill Family of Tharston, Norfolk Co., England, and Southold, Suffolk Co., New York (1898) (archive.org full text), pp. 7-10
sourceRefs.supports: Tuthill line to Anna Symmes Harrison

sourceRefs.citation: Curtiss C. Gardiner, Lion Gardiner and his Descendants (1890) (archive.org full text), pp. 118-121, 131-132, 148-149
sourceRefs.supports: Smith-Gardiner line to Julia Tyler; David Gardiner's death

sourceRefs.citation: Wikipedia, 'Julia Gardiner Tyler' (intro via MediaWiki API)

title: The spymaster who married his cousin
body:
Abraham Woodhull of Setauket, 'Samuel Culper Sr.' of Washington's Culper Ring, was a great-great-grandson of Bull Smith: his mother Margaret was a daughter of Edmund Smith, son of Adam, son of Bull. In 1781 he married Mary Smith, whose mother Anna was also a daughter of Edmund Smith, by his second wife, so the bride and groom were half-first cousins. Both of them are John's 3rd cousins 8 times removed.

A Topping connection sometimes claimed for the Woodhulls rests on Temperance, wife of Richard Woodhull II. The 1904 Woodhull Genealogy names her as a Fordham, and Capt. Thomas Topping had no daughter Temperance, so that route is doubtful.

sourceRefs.citation: Mary Gould Woodhull & Francis Bowes Stevens, Woodhull Genealogy: The Woodhull Family in England and America (1904) (archive.org full text), pp. 69-70, 266

title: Titanic, a rooftop murder, and Job Smith's descendants
body:
Judge J. Lawrence Smith of Smithtown (1816-1889) descended from John's ancestor Job Smith through Job's son Job 2d, whose daughter Anna married Ebenezer Smith; their son Richard 4th was the judge's grandfather. That makes the judge John's 4th cousin 6 times removed, closer than the route through his mother that was recorded before.

Two of the judge's children ended up in the headlines. His daughter Bessie married the architect Stanford White, who was shot dead by Harry K. Thaw on the roof of Madison Square Garden in June 1906. Her brother James Clinch Smith saw the shooting. Six years later James died in the sinking of the Titanic. Augustus Saint-Gaudens's marble bust and bronze medallion of Bessie are now at the Metropolitan Museum, which has released the images as CC0.

sourceRefs.citation: W. S. Pelletreau (ed.), Records of the Town of Smithtown (1898), Google scan (archive.org full text; used where the other scan's OCR drops text), App. pp. 465-466

title: A Bull Smith grandson who swore Long Island to the King
body: Col. Abraham Gardiner of East Hampton, husband of Bull Smith's great-granddaughter Mary Smith, sided with the Crown during the British occupation of Long Island. Gardiner's 1890 family history says he administered the oath of allegiance to the King in East Hampton in 1776; Sabine lists him among the Loyalists; and Major John André was quartered in his house. Meanwhile his kinsman Caleb Smith of Hauppauge was refusing to take the same oath. Gardiner's daughter Mary married the patriot magistrate Isaac Thompson of Sagtikos Manor, and his great-granddaughter Julia became First Lady.

sourceRefs.citation: Curtiss C. Gardiner, Lion Gardiner and his Descendants (1890) (archive.org full text), pp. 118-121

title: Captain Kidd's sailors and the Blydenburgh mill
body: According to Pelletreau's Blydenburgh notes, Joseph Blydenburgh 1st, who married Bull Smith's granddaughter Deborah, outfitted seamen for Captain William Kidd's Adventure Galley in 1696, before Kidd turned pirate. The family later ran the mill at the head of the Nissequogue, where Isaac Blydenburgh, Deborah's great-grandson, was a partner in 1798. Not every Blydenburgh is a cousin: Joseph's later children by his second wife descend from no Smith.

sourceRefs.citation: W. S. Pelletreau (ed.), Records of the Town of Smithtown (1898), Appendix (archive.org full text, scans recordsoftownofs00smitrich and recordstownsmit00pellgoog), App. pp. 483-486
sourceRefs.supports: Blydenburgh genealogy and Kidd outfitting note

title: Father and son who married two sisters
body: Bull Smith's daughter Elizabeth married William Lawrence of Flushing as his second wife and, after his death, Philip Carteret, governor of New Jersey. Lawrence's son William Jr. married Elizabeth's sister Deborah Smith in 1680, so the son's wife was his stepmother's sister. Thomas Lawrence's 1858 family history follows the descendants: Mayor Cornelius W. Lawrence, Hudson founder David Lawrence (a friend of Benjamin Franklin), Rear Admiral Daniel L. Braine, and through Capt. Effingham Lawrence of Trinity House, the English baronet Sir Willoughby Jones. The same book claims that Elizabethtown, New Jersey was named for Elizabeth; that claim is unverified.

sourceRefs.citation: Thomas Lawrence, Historical Genealogy of the Lawrence Family (1858) (archive.org full text), pp. 25-27, 46-56
sourceRefs.supports: Elizabeth and Deborah Smith's marriages; descendants

title: Neighbours on the South Shore: the Tuthills of Fireplace Neck and the Smiths of Moriches
body:
By 1721 James Tuthill, a Southold man, had settled at Brookhaven's south shore. The town laid out land to him on 'the other half of Dayton's Right' beside his Chestnut Pound land, and by 1737 he held the westernmost of the fifteen-acre lots in Fireplace Neck, 'at South'. That June the town commissioners laid a new four-rod highway along the north ends of those lots at the request of 'Jeames Tuttel' and his neighbours. In 1741 he sat with Isaac Browne, William Smith and Richard Woodhull as an arbitrator in a town dispute.

A few miles to the east, at Moriches, lived James Smith, a grandson of Richard 'Bull' Smith, with his wife Jerusha Topping and their large family: Matthew, Ezekiel, Zebulon, Austin, Nathaniel, Francis, Eunice, Keturah, Temperance and Jeremiah. In November 1752 James Tuthill's son John married Temperance Smith. Within a few years the young couple, the Smith brothers Austin and Francis, and James Tuthill himself had all moved up the Hudson to Woodbury Clove and New Windsor in Orange and Ulster counties. There Temperance's daughter Keturah grew up and married Ensign Thomas Lamoreaux.

sourceRefs.citation: Records of the Town of Brookhaven (printed 1880), pp. 113, 139-140, 147-148
Pelletreau, Records of the Town of Smithtown (1898), App. p. 479
sourceRefs.supports: James Smith of Moriches and his children

sourceRefs.citation: C. H. Weygant, The Family Record (1897), pp. 144-145
sourceRefs.supports: the Smith brothers at Woodbury Clove

title: A Highland patent before the migration?
body: Weygant's 1897 family history says that James Smith, son of Job, 'secured a patent for 2,000 acres of the annulled Capt. Evans grant' in 1722, in Ulster County 'adjoining the lands of Thomas Nixon and Patrick MacKnight'. Weygant thought it lay in the present town of Montgomery, Orange County, a few miles north-west of Smith's Clove, and noted that James never settled on it. The printed Calendar of Land Papers confirms a petition by a James Smith for 2,000 acres of vacant land on 29 Sept 1721, and a survey for him of 2,000 acres of the former Evans tract on 14 Dec 1722. If this James is Johnny's ancestor, as Weygant believed, his sons' move to Woodbury Clove a generation later was not a leap into the unknown. The family had been eyeing Highland land since the 1720s. The identification is not proven, since the calendar does not give his residence.

sourceRefs.citation: C. H. Weygant, The Family Record (1897), p. 144
Calendar of N.Y. Colonial Manuscripts, Indorsed Land Papers (1864), pp. 152, 166

title: How William Wells's widow became 'Mary Youngs'
body: Family trees call William Wells's wife 'Mary Youngs, daughter of Rev. John Youngs', and so attach the whole Youngs and 'Horne' pedigree to Johnny's tree. The Southold town book shows where the idea came from. On 26 December 1678 'Mary Mapes of Southold ... the relect of William Wells ... lately desceased, and now wife to Thomas Mapes Junr' gave her house, a meadow at Oyster Pond and a lot of commonage to 'my son in law John Yongs, in right of his wife ... Mary Yongs his wife my daughter'. Thomas Mapes and young William Wells witnessed the deed. The Youngs in the story was her daughter's husband, not her father. The 1907 Youngs genealogy agrees: Rev. John Youngs had no daughter who married Wells. Mary's own maiden name is still unknown.

sourceRefs.citation: Southold Town Records, vol. 1 (1882), pp. 302-303
Youngs Family (1907), pp. 38-41

title: A staff sergeant lost over Italy, 1943
body:
Harry Meier, born in Wilkes-Barre in 1923, was the youngest son of the iron moulder Fred A. Meier and his wife Anna Mather, and a first cousin of John's grandfather James. His mother died in February 1940. That April the census found his father lodging in Washington, DC, working as a molder at the Navy Yard, and Harry enlisted there in April 1942.

Harry became a staff sergeant in the Army Air Forces. On 2 Jul 1943, about a week before the Allied invasion of Sicily, he was killed over southern Italy; the family tree places his death at Scorrano, near Lecce in Apulia. Back home the Wilkes-Barre Record Almanac for 1946 still listed him as 'missing'. His remains were brought home after the war and buried with his comrades, in a single group grave, at Zachary Taylor National Cemetery in Louisville, Kentucky, on 15 Feb 1950. Group burials of this kind usually mean an aircrew whose individual remains could not be told apart. His Missing Air Crew Report would name his aircraft, bomb group and crewmates.

sourceRefs.citation: FamilySearch Family Tree, Henry James "Harry" Meier (G7CS-G54)
Interment.net, Zachary Taylor National Cemetery, surnames McH–Mi
sourceRefs.supports: S/Sgt, AAF, d. 2 Jul 1943, group burial 15 Feb 1950

title: Born before the wedding: Munzingen, January 1862
body:
On 11 Jan 1862, at half past nine in the morning, Maria Anna Birkenmaier, a 24-year-old unmarried day labourer and daughter of the late village joiner Servatius Birkenmaier, gave birth to a son at Munzingen. Two days later, when the boy was baptized Friedrich, the young mason Friedrich Mayer came before the parish priest and the legal witnesses. He declared himself the father and asked that the child carry his surname with all the rights of an acknowledged child. The godparents were his own family: his brother-in-law Joseph Wenz, the village shoemaker, and his unmarried sister Sophie, then in service in Freiburg.

Nine months later, on 20 Oct 1862, Friedrich and Maria Anna married at Munzingen. About six years and three more children later, the family sailed for Pennsylvania. The boy born in January 1862 grew up as Fred Meier of Hazleton. He still gave his birthday as '11 January 1862' when he married Annie Wenner there in 1886.

sourceRefs.citation: Landesarchiv BW, L 10 Nr. 1591 (Munzingen), Geburtsbuch 1862 No. 2 (images 431–432)
Luzerne County marriage license docket No. 714 (1886), image on FS G7GQ-XGX

title: Godparents from both families: the Mayer and Birkenmaier christenings, 1862–1864
body:
The Munzingen registers show how Friedrich Mayer and Maria Anna Birkenmaier's families closed ranks around the young couple before they left for America. Their first son, Friedrich, was born in January 1862 before they married. His godparents came from the Mayer side: the shoemaker Joseph Wenz, husband of Friedrich's eldest sister, and Friedrich's sister Sophie, who came home from domestic service in Freiburg.

After the October 1862 wedding, their daughter Franziska (Frances) was baptized in March 1863 with one godparent from each side: Maria Anna's brother Joseph Birkenmaier, a 20-year-old day labourer who later emigrated to Sandusky, Ohio, and Friedrich's youngest sister Pauline, 22. In May 1864 it was Pauline's turn to need help. She bore a daughter, Christina, out of wedlock, and Friedrich and his sister Maria Anna Wenz stood godparents. Four months later Friedrich and Maria Anna's daughter Maria (Mary) was born, on 3 September 1864.

Within four years Friedrich, Maria Anna and their children were in Hazleton. Maria Anna's sister Karolina stayed behind and died unmarried in Munzingen in March 1869, aged 23. Her uncle Friedrich Heitzler, a citizen of Munzingen, had died in December 1865 far from home, near Lörrach.

sourceRefs.citation: Landesarchiv BW, Staatsarchiv Freiburg, L 10 Nr. 1591 (Munzingen, kath.), Geburtsbuch 1862 No. 2; 1863 No. 3; 1864 Nos. 9 and 15; Todtenbuch 1866 No. 1a; 1869 No. 5

title: A widower marries his late wife's niece, 1917
body: Sophia Gertrude Meier, the second-youngest of Friedrich and Maria Anna's children, married the Easton clerk George Thomas Duffin on 3 June 1903 and died at Easton in April 1909, aged 28. Eight years later, in January 1917, George married again in Luzerne County. His bride was Agatha Mary Rose, the daughter of Sophia's elder sister Mary (Meier) Rose of Hazleton, so his second wife was his first wife's niece. George and Agatha lived in Williams Township near Easton for decades. Both died in 1966.

sourceRefs.citation: Northampton County Marriage License No. 10968, Duffin × Meier, 1903 (FamilySearch image on G7GQ-XH5)

title: The president's son who was stolen from his grave (1878)
body:
When former Congressman John Scott Harrison, son of one president and father of another, died suddenly at his farm near North Bend, Ohio, in May 1878, his family already knew that grave robbers were working the area: a young neighbour's grave had just been emptied. They dug his grave unusually deep, lined it with brick, sank heavy cemented stones over the metal coffin and paid a man to watch it every night.

It was not enough. The next day his son John and grandson George Eaton went to Cincinnati with a search warrant to look for the neighbour's body at the Ohio Medical College. In a cellar used to receive cadavers they pulled up a rope hanging down a chute and found the naked body of an old man, his long grey beard cut off. As they were about to let it drop, the son saw the face and cried out that it was his father. The college janitor was arrested that evening, and the outrage helped bring about Ohio's anatomy law of 1881.

sourceRefs.citation: New York Herald, 31 May 1878, p.5, 'Body Snatching' (Chronicling America)
Wikipedia, 'John Scott Harrison'

title: Killed by lightning on his own road (1886)
body: George Lane Pringle, a twin born at Plymouth in 1822, farmed in Kingston all his life and never married. On 19 March 1886 an unusually early, violent spring thunderstorm swept the Wyoming Valley. He was walking along the road beside a farm he owned in Huntington Township when lightning struck and killed him. The news went out over the wire, and the next day the Washington Evening Star reported that 'George L. Pringle, an old and prominent resident of Kingston, was struck by lightning on the roadway and killed.' His younger brother Alexander, a Wilkes-Barre schoolmaster turned banker, had died five years earlier after a stroke in church.

sourceRefs.citation: Harvey, The Harvey Book (1899), pp.137-138
Evening Star (Washington), 20 Mar 1886, p.5

title: Fined one cent for defending Washington
body: George Palmer Ransom marched as a teenager in his father's company at Millstone, Bound Brook, Brandywine and Germantown. His father was killed at the Battle of Wyoming. In December 1780 Indians seized him while he sat, in his best uniform, courting at a neighbour's fireside. He escaped from a prison island in the St. Lawrence by swimming the river. Decades later, as an old colonel in Plymouth, he heard a young man speak disparagingly of General Washington and knocked him down. Brought into court, he pleaded guilty without a lawyer. Judge Scott stood up and left the case to his two associate judges, both old soldiers. They asked Ransom where he had been in 1777, 1778, 1779 and 1780, and he answered: in Washington's army, on the march to Wyoming, with Sullivan against the Indians, and a prisoner on the St. Lawrence. 'And did you knock the fellow down?' 'I did so and would do it again under like provocation.' The sentence was a fine of one cent, with the prosecutor to pay the costs. It was written into Quarter Sessions Docket No. 1.

sourceRefs.citation: Harvey & Smith, A History of Wilkes-Barre, vol. V (1929), Judge Thomas Burnside Scott section
sourceRefs.supports: the assault case and one-cent fine (Quarter Sessions Docket No. 1)

sourceRefs.citation: H. B. Wright, Historical Sketches of Plymouth, Luzerne Co., Penna. (1873), ch. VII-VIII (pp.156-241), p.283 and the pound passage; portrait facing p.240
sourceRefs.supports: birth at Canaan, Conn., 1761; Revolutionary service as orderly-sergeant (Millstone, Bound Brook, Germantown, Brandywine); capture on 6 Dec 1780; imprisonment and escape; died in his red mansion house in Plymouth; daughter married Charles C. Curtis; portrait at 85. Wright was his next-door neighbor for 20 years.

title: The day the dance pavilion fell into the creek (1935)
body: Croop's Glen at Hunlock Creek grew out of the Croop family's mill seat. By the 1920s Benjamin F. Croop had turned it into a resort with picnic grounds, pony rides and a dance pavilion built over the creek, and it drew excursion crowds from the whole valley. On the afternoon of 29 June 1935 about 400 men, women and children packed the old pavilion to watch a baby contest. The structure gave way and dropped thirty or forty feet into the shallow creek below. The Associated Press reported a hundred injured, some perhaps fatally, though none were killed outright and none drowned. The news ran in papers as far away as Washington and McAllen, Texas.

sourceRefs.citation: McAllen Daily Monitor (McAllen, Texas), 30 Jun 1935, p.1 (AP, Wilkes-Barre, 29 Jun)
Harvey & Smith, A History of Wilkes-Barre, vol. VI (1930), Stanley Carson Croop biography

title: Three Huguenot weddings in New York, summer 1693
body: In the summer of 1693 the French Church of New York, made up of refugees who had fled Louis XIV's persecution of Protestants, recorded a run of weddings that tied the Mercereau family to other exiles. On 16 July 1693 Jean La Tourette, from Osse in Béarn, married Marie Mercereau, and on the same day Josué Mercereau married Marie Chadaine of Saintonge. Three weeks later, on 6 August, Daniel Mercereau married Suzanne Marie Doucinet of La Rochelle. Over the following years the same register records the baptisms of their children: Marie, Jean, Pierre and David La Tourette; Marie and Josué Mercereau; Daniel, Susanne Marie and Marianne Mercereau. The Josué Mercereau baptized in 1696 was the grandfather of Joshua Mersereau, who ran a spy ring on Staten Island for Washington.

sourceRefs.citation: Collections of the Huguenot Society of America, vol. 1 (1886): Registers of the French Church of New York
sourceRefs.supports: marriages and baptisms (published transcription of the church register)

title: A will that settles a mother: Captain Thomas Davenport, 1746
body:
On 10 October 1746 Thomas Davenport of Philipse's Precinct, the 'Captain' of the Dutchess County highway commission, was 'sick and weak in body' and made his will. It shows a man with two families. The grown children of his first marriage (sons Thomas and William, and the children of his married daughters Sarah Mandeville, Mary Henion and Elizabeth Nelson) received small fixed sums. The remainder went to seven young children, Oliver, Charity, Phebe, Robert, Hannah, Stephen and Abigail, who were to be paid as they came of age, the boys taking double shares. Until then his wife Elizabeth was to keep the farm improvements, the household goods and an enslaved person 'for bringing up my Children'.

Thomas recovered and lived another thirteen years. In August 1759, a few months before his death, he gave a family Bible to his grandson. The will has a quiet consequence for John's line: Charity, later the wife of the Huguenot descendant John Lamoreaux, was one of those minors in 1746. She was therefore the daughter of the second wife, Elizabeth, and was unmarried at the time. By 1752 she was 'Charity Lamoree, wife of John Lamoree', when her father deeded her land in Goshen precinct beside her brother Oliver.

sourceRefs.citation: Giles, Thomas Davenport, Pioneer, and His Descendants: transcript of the will of Thomas Davenport, 10 Oct 1746

title: Neighbours in New Cornwall, 1790
body:
The first federal census of 1790 caught the Lamoreaux family still in the hills of Orange County, New York, a few years before most of them moved to the Wyoming Valley. On one page of New Cornwall's return are Peter Lomereaux and John Lomereaux. John's household held four men, three women or girls and three enslaved people. Further down the page are Oliver Davenport, John's brother-in-law, and a David Prindle with a young family.

Within a decade John's son Thomas Lamoreaux and his daughter Charity (wife of Thomas Davenport) were in Plymouth, Pennsylvania. Thomas's daughter Martha married Samuel Pringle, or Prindle, whose family seems to have known the Lamoreaux family in Orange County first. Benjamin and David Prindle served in the same First Orange County militia regiment as the Lamoreaux men during the Revolution.

sourceRefs.citation: 1790 US census, New Cornwall, Orange Co., NY, p.382
New York in the Revolution as Colony and State (1898), p.253

title: Buried with a sermon: Caspar Grub of Berschweiler, 1671
body: Caspar Grub was born in 1616 or 1617 and grew up during the Thirty Years' War, which left much of the Palatinate empty. He married Elisabetha Birgert of Fockenberg-Limbach in 1642 and settled at Berschweiler. Early on Sunday morning, 30 April 1671, he died there. The next day he was buried 'mit einer Leichpredigt', with a funeral sermon, a mark of standing in the village. The Lauterecken pastor wrote in the register that he had lived 53 years, 11 months and 3 days. His son Johann Peter, then sixteen, later moved to Jettenbach and became a church elder there. Johann Peter's grandsons Andreas and Johann Peter sailed for Philadelphia in 1753 and 1754.

sourceRefs.citation: Lauterecken Lutheran parish register, burials 1671 (Caspar Grub)
